worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: From a sound to a meaning
worked.scenario: You hear a brief tone and recognize it as a phone notification.
steps: The vibration is a stimulus. Hair cells in the inner ear are mechanoreceptors that respond to the resulting movement.
The sensory pathway carries information to the brain. Becoming aware of the tone is sensation.
Recognizing the tone as a notification is perception. The brain gives meaning to the information.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Follow a different sense
guided.instruction: Sunlight warms your skin. Complete the explanation.

items.prompt: Which receptor category detects the temperature change?
items.hint: Name what changes at the skin.
items.explanation: Thermoreceptors detect temperature change. The light source is not the same thing as the stimulus detected in this skin example.

items.prompt: You become aware that your skin feels warm. Which term fits this conscious experience?
items.hint: Distinguish detection at a receptor from awareness in the brain.
items.explanation: Sensation is becoming aware of the input. Reception began when the receptors detected the change.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Light getting in is only one step
worked.scenario: An eye has a clear cornea and lens, but its photoreceptors are damaged.
steps: The clear cornea and lens may still allow light through and focus it on the retina.
The retina contains rods and cones. Damaged receptors may not convert the light into normal signals.
Light must reach the retina, but that alone does not produce vision. The receptors and the pathway carrying their information must also work.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Complete the light route
guided.instruction: Use the sequence cornea → aqueous humour → pupil → lens → vitreous humour → retina.

items.prompt: Which structure changes the size of the opening in that route?
items.hint: The pupil is an opening within a ring of muscle.
items.explanation: Iris muscles change pupil size and control how much light enters.

items.prompt: Which part contains the receptors that detect the light?
items.hint: Clear materials let light pass; receptors detect it.
items.explanation: Rods and cones are in the retina. The humours transmit light and the sclera protects the eye.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Looking from far away to nearby
worked.scenario: You stop looking at a distant clock and look down at a book.
steps: Near vision needs stronger bending of incoming light.
The ciliary muscle contracts, reducing the pull of the suspensory ligaments.
The lens becomes rounder. Its stronger focusing effect helps form a clear image on the retina.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Now reverse the change
guided.instruction: You look from the book back to the distant clock.

items.prompt: The ciliary muscle relaxes. What happens to ligament tension?
items.hint: A distant object needs a flatter lens.
items.explanation: Relaxation allows the suspensory ligaments to become more taut.

items.prompt: What follows the increased pull?
items.answer: The lens flattens and bends light less strongly
options: The lens flattens and bends light less strongly
The lens rounds and bends light more strongly
items.hint: Trace tension → shape → focusing effect.
items.explanation: Greater ligament tension stretches the lens flatter, reducing its focusing power for distant vision.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Separate incoming light from outgoing information
worked.scenario: Trace a simplified three-layer retina.
steps: Incoming light passes the ganglion-cell layer, then the bipolar-cell layer, before reaching rods and cones.
Rods and cones detect the light and change their signalling. Information passes to bipolar cells and then ganglion cells.
Ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve. This route carries neural information, not light.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Fill the two routes
guided.instruction: Choose the missing stage in each route.

items.prompt: Incoming light: ganglion-cell layer → ____ → rods and cones.
items.hint: Think about the middle retinal layer.
items.explanation: Light passes through the bipolar-cell layer before reaching the photoreceptors.

items.prompt: Neural information: rods and cones → bipolar cells → ____ → optic nerve.
items.hint: Which cells send their axons into the optic nerve?
items.explanation: Ganglion cells receive information from the retinal circuit, and their axons form the optic nerve.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Locate the first affected step
worked.scenario: Fluid in the middle ear reduces how well the eardrum and ossicles move.
steps: The problem affects mechanical transmission before the receptors.
Less vibration can reach the oval window and cochlear fluid.
Hair-cell stimulation may be reduced even if the hair cells and auditory nerve are not damaged.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Movement becomes neural information
guided.instruction: Follow the energy through the hearing pathway.

items.prompt: Immediately after the stapes moves the oval window, what happens?
items.answer: Pressure waves move through cochlear fluid
options: Pressure waves move through cochlear fluid
The auditory nerve carries sound waves
items.hint: The inner ear is fluid-filled.
items.explanation: Oval-window movement creates fluid pressure waves in the cochlea.

items.prompt: Which event performs the sensory conversion?
items.answer: Bending of hair-cell projections changes cell signalling
options: Bending of hair-cell projections changes cell signalling
items.hint: Choose the receptor event rather than a supporting structure.
items.explanation: Hair cells transduce movement into changed electrical and chemical signalling, which affects auditory nerve fibres.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Separate a louder note from a higher note
worked.scenario: A recorded tone becomes louder while its frequency stays constant.
steps: Frequency has not changed, so its pitch stays approximately the same.
The larger pressure variation means the wave amplitude has increased.
The nervous system represents the stronger input through activity patterns, not taller individual action potentials.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Compare two described waves
guided.instruction: These are invented comparison values, not a hearing test: A has 4 cycles in 0.01 s; B has 8 cycles in 0.01 s. They have equal amplitudes.

items.prompt: Which sound has the higher pitch?
options: They must have the same pitch
items.hint: Compare cycle counts over the same time.
items.explanation: B has more cycles in the same interval, so its frequency and expected pitch are higher.

items.prompt: What does equal amplitude support in this simplified comparison?
options: B must be twice as loud
items.hint: Amplitude and frequency describe different wave properties.
items.explanation: Equal amplitudes support a similar-loudness comparison here. The cycle counts still differ, so pitch differs.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Classify straight-line acceleration
worked.scenario: An elevator starts moving upward while a passenger keeps their head facing forward.
steps: The described change is vertical straight-line acceleration, not head rotation.
The saccule is especially relevant. Acceleration shifts its weighted otolithic membrane relative to hair cells.
Bending the hair-cell projections changes signalling about the movement.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Compare turning with moving straight
guided.instruction: Use the structure that matches each kind of movement.

items.prompt: Your head starts turning to look over your shoulder. Which mechanism fits?
items.answer: Fluid movement bends a cupula in a semicircular canal
options: Fluid movement bends a cupula in a semicircular canal
A weighted membrane in the saccule detects a sound wave
items.hint: The change is rotation.
items.explanation: Relative fluid movement in a semicircular canal bends the cupula and hair-cell projections.

items.prompt: A vehicle starts moving straight forward. Which structure is especially relevant?
items.hint: Horizontal acceleration differs from a turn.
items.explanation: The utricle helps detect horizontal linear acceleration through movement of its weighted otolithic membrane.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Model a complete investigation plan
worked.scenario: Plan only: compare touch discrimination on a fingertip and the forearm. Do not perform the test.
steps: Question: Does the smallest separation reported as two contacts differ between these body regions?
Prediction: The fingertip will distinguish closer contacts because its sensory representation is generally more precise.
Manipulated variable: body region. Responding variable: the smallest separation reported as two contacts, measured in millimetres.
Controls: use the same contact method, pressure, contact duration and instructions. Plan repeated trials with the same participant and more than one participant before making broad conclusions.
Safety and evidence: this is a written plan only. No physical testing or sharp objects are required. A completed data table would need real observations; a prediction is not a result.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Complete part of a second plan
guided.instruction: A written plan compares the palm with the forearm. The question concerns the smallest separation reported as two contacts.

items.prompt: What is the manipulated variable?
items.hint: Identify what the plan deliberately changes.
items.explanation: The plan changes which body region is considered. The smallest reported separation is the measured response.

items.prompt: The plan changes both body region and contact pressure. What needs fixing?
items.answer: Keep pressure consistent so the region comparison is fair
options: Keep pressure consistent so the region comparison is fair
Record the prediction as the result
items.hint: More than one changing factor makes the result harder to explain.
items.explanation: Keeping pressure consistent helps isolate the effect of body region. Repeated trials can then help assess consistency.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Turn a list into an explanation
worked.scenario: A student writes only “pancreas, insulin, blood glucose.”
steps: Add the trigger: blood glucose rises after a meal.
Add the response: pancreatic beta cells release insulin into the blood.
Add target effects: responsive tissues increase glucose uptake and storage. Blood glucose moves back toward its usual range.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Connect the parts
guided.instruction: Use this supplied case: blood glucose rises; the pancreas releases insulin; responsive cells take up more glucose.

items.prompt: Which part is the trigger?
items.hint: The trigger starts the response.
items.explanation: The rise in glucose is the starting change. Hormone release and uptake are later steps.

items.prompt: Why does insulin not affect every cell in exactly the same way?
items.answer: Cells differ in their receptors and responses
options: Cells differ in their receptors and responses
All hormones act only on their gland of origin
items.hint: Delivery and response are different things.
items.explanation: Blood distributes insulin, but target-cell receptors and response mechanisms determine its effects.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Predict where the receptor is
worked.scenario: A hormone is described as water soluble and unable to pass directly through the membrane’s lipid layer.
steps: The hormone is unlikely to reach an internal receptor by passing directly through the membrane.
It can bind to a receptor at the cell surface.
The receptor passes a signal to processes inside the cell. The hormone itself need not enter.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Compare the two mechanisms
guided.instruction: Focus on receptor location, not simply how long a response lasts.

items.prompt: Where does a steroid hormone such as cortisol bind its receptor?
options: On every cell regardless of receptor type
items.hint: Steroids can enter target cells.
items.explanation: Steroid hormones bind intracellular receptors and can influence gene expression.

items.prompt: A water-soluble hormone is present, but its surface receptor is missing. What is the likely result?
items.answer: The usual response to that hormone is reduced or absent
options: The usual response to that hormone is reduced or absent
The cell must respond more strongly
items.hint: The message must be recognized.
items.explanation: Normal delivery does not replace the missing receptor needed to start the usual response.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: An upward response can be negative feedback
worked.scenario: Blood glucose falls. Glucagon helps the liver release glucose, raising blood glucose.
steps: The starting change is a decrease in blood glucose.
The response increases blood glucose toward its usual range.
The response opposes the starting decrease. Therefore this is negative feedback.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Use the starting change
guided.instruction: Decide from the relationship between the stimulus and response.

items.prompt: Body temperature rises, and a response helps lower it. Which feedback fits?
items.hint: Does the response oppose or strengthen the rise?
items.explanation: Lowering temperature opposes the starting rise, so the feedback is negative.

items.prompt: Cervical stretch strengthens contractions, which increase cervical stretch. Which feedback fits?
items.hint: The response adds to the original stimulus.
items.explanation: More stretch produces a response that increases stretch. The loop reinforces the starting change until its endpoint.

worked.title: Answer the verb in the question
worked.scenario: Two questions ask where ADH is made and where it is released into blood.
steps: “Made” asks where the molecule is produced: neurons in the hypothalamus.
ADH travels along axons to the posterior pituitary, where it is stored.
“Released” asks where the stored hormone enters the blood: the posterior pituitary.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Compare the two pituitary routes
guided.instruction: Use the route, production site and release site together.

items.prompt: Which route carries hypothalamic regulatory hormones to the anterior pituitary?
items.hint: The anterior pituitary receives chemical control signals through blood.
items.explanation: Releasing and inhibiting hormones travel in the connecting portal blood vessels.

items.prompt: Milk is being produced, but the question concerns its release. Which hormone has that role?
items.hint: Production and release are different processes.
items.explanation: Oxytocin supports milk ejection. Prolactin supports milk production.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Use the growth-plate condition
worked.scenario: Two cases describe excessive hGH. One has open growth plates and one has closed growth plates.
steps: Open plates allow long bones to lengthen. Excess hGH can produce gigantism.
Closed plates do not allow the same growth in height. Excess hGH can enlarge bones and soft tissues in other ways, producing acromegaly.
The different outcome follows from the target tissue’s condition, not a different hormone name.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Complete the growth pathway
guided.instruction: Use the normal pathway before interpreting a growth problem.

items.prompt: Which organ can release growth factors in response to hGH?
items.hint: Separate the hGH release site from the growth-factor target.
items.explanation: The anterior pituitary releases hGH. The liver can respond by releasing growth factors.

items.prompt: A case states that growth plates are closed. Which excess-hGH outcome fits?
items.hint: Closed growth plates change how tissue can grow.
items.explanation: With closed plates, bones and soft tissues can enlarge without the same increase in height.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Trace water conservation
worked.scenario: A case describes water loss, increasingly concentrated blood and normally responsive kidneys.
steps: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the concentration change.
More ADH is released from the posterior pituitary. Collecting ducts become more permeable to water.
More water returns to the blood, leaving a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.
The correction reduces the original stimulus for extra ADH release.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Fill the missing links
guided.instruction: Keep the blood and the forming urine separate.

items.prompt: More ADH → more permeable collecting ducts → ____ water reabsorption.
items.hint: Water can cross the duct wall more easily.
items.explanation: Increased permeability allows more water to return from the forming urine to the blood.

items.prompt: With more water reabsorbed, what happens to urine?
items.answer: Its volume falls and it becomes more concentrated
options: Its volume falls and it becomes more concentrated
Its volume rises and it becomes more dilute
items.hint: Less water remains in the fluid leaving the kidney.
items.explanation: More water is conserved in the body, leaving less water in the urine.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Follow feedback in a working pathway
worked.scenario: The thyroid, hypothalamus and pituitary are functioning. Thyroxine rises above its usual level.
steps: Thyroxine is the final hormone in this control pathway.
Its increased feedback tends to reduce TRH release and TSH release.
Less TSH means less thyroid stimulation. This restrains further thyroxine production.

guided.title: Complete the normal pathway first
guided.instruction: Use the sequence you just learned before considering a damaged gland.

items.hint: Choose the hormone released by the anterior pituitary.
items.explanation: TSH is thyroid-stimulating hormone. The thyroid responds by releasing thyroxine.

items.prompt: Thyroxine falls and the hypothalamus and pituitary still function. What tends to happen to TSH?
items.answer: It rises as thyroxine feedback weakens
options: It rises as thyroxine feedback weakens
It must fall because thyroxine fell
items.hint: Less final hormone means less inhibition of the working control glands.
items.explanation: With weaker thyroxine feedback, the pituitary can increase TSH release.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Follow a decrease in blood calcium
worked.scenario: Blood calcium falls below its usual range.
steps: The parathyroid glands release more PTH.
PTH promotes calcium release from bone and calcium reabsorption by the kidneys. It also supports vitamin-D activation, increasing intestinal calcium absorption.
The combined actions raise blood calcium and reduce the original stimulus.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Name the calcium movement
guided.instruction: Complete the mechanism rather than just choosing a hormone name.

items.prompt: Returning calcium from kidney-tubule fluid to the blood is called…
items.hint: The substance is being recovered from forming urine.
items.explanation: Kidney reabsorption returns calcium to the blood, conserving it.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly compares the main directions of the two hormones?
items.answer: PTH raises blood calcium; calcitonin tends to lower it
options: PTH raises blood calcium; calcitonin tends to lower it
Calcitonin raises it while PTH lowers it
items.hint: They have opposing effects.
items.explanation: The opposite effects make them antagonistic hormones; their regulatory importance is not identical.

worked.title: Locate the neural-to-hormonal change
worked.scenario: A sudden threat activates sympathetic signals reaching the adrenal medulla.
steps: The incoming signal reaches the medulla along neurons.
The medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood.
Target responses support rapid action, including increased heart activity and glucose availability.

guided.title: Finish the rapid stress route

It stores all available glucose away permanently

worked.title: Compare after a meal with between meals
worked.scenario: Compare a rise in blood glucose after eating with a fall between meals.
steps: After a meal, beta cells release more insulin. Glucose uptake and storage help lower blood glucose.
Between meals, alpha cells release more glucagon. The liver releases glucose, helping raise blood glucose.
Both responses oppose their starting changes, so both use negative feedback.

Glucose is removed from blood only to make more glycogen
All glucose is trapped inside beta cells
